TL;DR: Ever wanted a Surface Tablet, but didn't want to use Windows? This Asus CM3 might be what you're looking for. And the stylus and keyboard are actually included. Chrome OS lets you run apps from the Google Play store now, which makes it more useful than ever, but there can be a bit of a learning curve if you're not used to it and some apps are just not optimized for "laptop" mode, not to mention stylus use. Underpowered for the price; but you get a very portable form factor with a lot of versatility.

Form and Build:
The tablet is a great size for carrying with you. It's a bit heavy, but it's compact and well-contained with magnetic closures. It will also fit in some tablet sleeves, though it might be too thick a package for the especially svelte ones. Ultimately, it's pretty easy to keep in a backpack, tote or even a larger purse. The tablet on its own is very angular, with rounded corners and is build very solidly. I do like the gray cover on the back that also serves as a multi-directional kickstand, but as it's attached only via magnets, it does sometimes slide around when given a good jostle. The keyboard attaches tightly, also using a magnetic attachment similar to what you'd find on a Surface tablet. It snaps satisfyingly into place and does take a little effort to pull away from the tablet.

The keyboard is the weak link, here. While the back cover is pleasant, the typing surface feels cheap and plasticky. They keys are clicky and you're typing on a REAL keyboard, not a haptic one, which is definitely welcome. But feedback is hollow and at times you feel like you might snap the keyboard should your typing grow too passionate.

It's great that the stylus is included and I like that it's "garaged," but you are almost guaranteed to break a nail trying to get that stylus out of its hidey-hole. Samsung does a much better job with its garaged pens than Asus has done here.

The tablet/laptop has only one USB-C port and one headphone jack, both of which work. It is disappointing that it does not have expandability via MicroSD like many Android tablets and even other Chromebooks, especially considering you'll probably be downloading Google Play apps. While there's a good deal of storage here for a Chromebook (my first Chromebook years ago only had 16GB hard drive space--everything was supposed to be in the cloud...), that expandability would have been welcome.

Screen and Stylus Input:
The screen actually looks great. Images are crisp and videos play with good clarity. Text is easy to read. Touch features work well, especially on Google Play apps made for it. Stylus input is a little more inconsistent. If you're used to using a Surface pen or Apple Pencil, you'll likely be disappointed by the writing and drawing experience on this tablet. I've found that a lot of the inconsistency stems from software--it's a trick to find the best apps for writing and drawing, and hitting that balance between picking up the stylus input and effective palm rejection. This is not a game you have to play with an iPad/Apple Pencil combo. The screen really needs a paper-like screen protector if you'll be making heavy use of the stylus.

Performance:
Chrome OS has some really great elements. I like the automatic updates and cloud integration. A lot here just works, especially if you're deep in the Google environment. I also like how easy it is to set up multiple profiles. I am easily able to switch between my personal and work profiles and have all of that stuff separate. Start up is fast and I haven't run into any serious issues of the Chromebook getting hung up on processes it couldn't handle. The only issue I did have was when trying to play a purchased video in the YouTube app and spent a good deal of time trying to figure out how to clear the app cache--it's different from Chrome browser and from the Google Play app, so... like I said, learning curve. My only other issue is with volume control. The volume rocker works--you can see the volume control appear on the screen when you press it--but it doesn't really seem to do anything. I kept trying to turn down the volume of a video playing, and it went from too loud to muted and nothing in between. I had to fine tune the volume in each individual app I played media in using the software slider.

The bottom line:
There are cheaper Chromebooks out there. If you're looking for "a Chromebook" because you want to run Chrome OS, you might be able to get what you want at a better price point. Consider the ASUS CM3 if the form factor in particular appeals to you. It is versatile--you get a tablet, stylus, keyboard/laptop situation all in one machine that is easy to take with you or sit on the couch with.

[[VIDEOID:9b8bc93cf53a92f001896b17ed21144c]] Review model: Lenovo Legion 5 15 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" FHD (1920 x 1080) Display, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB NVMe SSD, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050Ti, Windows 10H, 82JW0012US, Phantom Blue

TL;DR: I’ve recently tried out three gaming computers on three tiers: a high-end Alienware m15 R4(10th gen i7 with an RTX 3080), a more entry-level Acer Nitro 5 (10th gen i5 with an RTX 3050) and this mid-range Lenovo Legion 5. Out of the 3, the Lenovo Legion (Ryzen 7 with an RTX 3050ti) is actually my favorite. It comes out on top as the best value, with very impressive overall performance and excellent features with few trade-offs.

Form & Build:
This computer looks fantastic. The subtle navy blue color differentiates the Legion from a lot of other “gaming” computers. The matte finishes hide fingerprints without looking cheap. The monitor hinge is inset from the rear of the computer by a couple of inches making the whole machine feel a lot more stable when the monitor is open--it never feels wobbly or top-heavy. The computer is beefy without being so heavy that you can’t have this thing on your lap (on a good lapdesk, natch).

Keyboard & touchpad:
If you’ve ever used a Lenovo Thinkpad for work, the keyboard on the Legion will feel very familiar. The main keyboard keys are well-sized and very comfortable to type on. They have good travel with just enough clickiness. Very quiet. I do like that there’s a full number pad. The number pad keys seem like they are slightly smaller than the alpha keys, which makes for a little bit of a lopsided look, but you get used to it very quickly. If you don’t often use the number pad, you barely notice. The touchpad is comfortable and responsive, but could be larger. You’ll likely be using a regular mouse for games, anyway. The RGB backlighting on this laptop is beautiful. There is a selection of different zones and color schemes (it’s not expansive, but the light pastel-y scheme was my favorite), so you can probably find a style and brightness that you like.

Display:
The screen looks great and even when I wanted something bigger, I had no problem hooking it up to my monitor via HDMI. The bottom bezel is large, lifting the screen a bit and giving you a better viewing angle. The matte finish of the screen succeeds at reducing glare.

Graphics:
Really impressive given the relatively low-end 3050Ti. The combination of the 3050Ti and the Ryzen 7 CPU seems to be a sweet spot for laptop gaming. Honestly, under every-day play conditions it was hard to tell the difference between my Alienware with a 3080 and the Legion. Based on my play tests with World of Warcraft: Shadowlands and Code Vein, the biggest tradeoff with the Legion (Ryzen/3050Ti) and Alienware (i7/3080) is in ray tracing and anti-aliasing. When ray tracing and anti-aliasing were turned off, the Legion frame rates were almost as good as the Alienware, but I did have the occasional screen-tearing issue, and light bouncing off shiny objects (ray tracing) was not nearly as cool. I also did turn down some distance detail to reduce the rare stutter.

In return for a surprisingly meager reduction in visual quality, the Legion gave me outstanding temperature performance. I was totally impressed by the Ryzen 7 in terms of temperature control. I was able to have the Legion out on my lap desk questing while watching TV on the couch. I have never been able to do that with the Alienware. After playing for hours, the keyboard on the Legion never heated up noticeably and the bottom of the computer remained cool to the touch. The Legion effectively ventilates heat through the rear and sides using fans. With my feet up, I could definitely feel that hot air output on my legs, but that heat was consistently moving away from the laptop. The power brick, however, DOES heat up quite a lot. Make sure it’s located somewhere away from metal and loose papers and can get good airflow.

TL; DR: The Acer Nitro 5 AN515-55-53E5 Gaming Laptop is an entry-level gaming-capable computer. Its out-of-the-box specs are underwhelming, but some can be upgraded, like RAM and hard drive space. The RTX 3050 is the cheapest house in the fancy neighborhood. It’s a solid starter GPU for current games, but temper your frame rate and detail expectations. The Comet Lake i5 CPU is capable, but can run hot. Get used to the fans. Don’t pay more than MSRP, given you’ll need to fork out some extra money on ram and another SSD to meet basic storage needs.

Form & Build:

The Nitro 5 is a big computer, but not so big that you couldn’t put it in a backpack and take it with you to a friend’s place. (Do people still have LAN parties? Good times…) The heavily plastic build keeps the weight down, but contributes to some questionable points of quality. For instance, pressing on the top of the lid when closed, there’s a lot of give. This can absorb impact if you drop it--feels like it could crack under the wrong force. The semi-gloss surfaces inside and out do pick up oils from the skin that are hard to get off and show as shiny spots.

There are some good input options, with 3 standard USB ports and a USB C port. There’s an ethernet port, too, as well as an HDMI output and a headphone/mic jack. The only port on the rear of the unit is the power jack, which is sort of awkwardly placed right in the middle, rather than off to the side. There is no Displayport output.

The fan can get quite loud to keep the unit cool. The CPU heats up, especially when gaming. The bottom of the computer stays relatively cool, thanks to the fans and ventilation to the rear and sides, but parts of the keyboard can get pretty warm. You can monitor CPU and GPU temperatures in the NItro app. There’s even a hotkey for it (top left of the number pad).

Keyboard, Touchpad and Screen:

The keyboard is well-sized. It’s nice to have a full number pad. The keys have good travel; they’re quiet and have solid feedback. Some of the keys are oddly sized/placed, like the right shift key, to make more room for the arrows and the number pad. The number pad has standard sized keys. The red backlighting can be adjusted for brightness, but not for color (unless there is some software controller that I haven’t been able to find yet). It can’t be changed in the Lenovo Vantage or Nitro app. The texture of the keys feels slightly rubberized, but smooth without being slippery. Trackpad is smooth and responsive. It’s a decent size, but I’d be comfortable with something a little larger. You’ll probably be using a mouse for gaming anyway.

The screen is okay. I like that it is slightly elevated with a larger bezel to the bottom--this makes it feel a little larger than it is and gives a better viewing angle. The matte finish is good for reducing glare. However, visually, it’s a bit washed out. Blacks and whites have a slight grayness to them and the screen never seems quite as bright as it could be. Make good use of that HDMI output and hook up to your favorite full-sized monitor.

Performance:

Gaming performance on the Nitro 5 is good enough for a lot of games. If you’re looking for a decent laptop to play League of Legends, WoW or Final Fantasy 14 with your friends, this one will definitely work. If you want to dominate in League, destroy your foes in PVP or need super high frame rates and detail for streaming… you might want to invest in something with higher specs, even with the upgradeability of this PC.

The factory SSD works really well. Games and programs load fast, starting up Windows after sleep/hibernate/shutdown is a breeze. The Nvidia Experience app will automatically optimize game settings based on your hardware, or you can manually tweak certain things based on your play style, which is really great. You can monitor resource use and temperatures using the Nitro app.

My current games of choice are World of Warcraft Shadowlands (2020) and Code Vein (2019). I’ve had to turn detail down a bit in both games for the sake of framerate, but they both still run very well. In WoW, I’m at medium-high custom settings (graphics slider is at 7, with some settings turned down a little lower, like spell effects, ground cover and water detail). I’m getting 60-80 fps depending the number of other players in an area. Code Vein is almost maxed out settings-wise. I turned down distance-detail and turned off ray tracing to improve framerates and responsiveness.

Download speeds are pretty impressive. A lot can depend on client-side factors (battle.net has much slower download speeds than Steam, for instance), but on Steam, I’ve been averaging 50mbs or about 3-4 GB/min., which is nothing to sneeze at. Glad I installed another hard drive to install those games on!

Upgrading:

You only get 8GB of RAM and a 256 GB SSD on this computer out of the box. These are the most lackluster specs… but, these are also the things you can upgrade. I successfully doubled my usable hard drive space by adding a cheap 240GB 2.5in SATA SSD into the open bay. There is also an OPEN RAM slot. You can slip an 8GB stick right into that open slot to double the ram or replace the ram and add more with 2x16 for a max of 32GB, which should speed up your overall performance quite a bit, especially if you do a lot of multitasking. These are, of course, going to be additional expenses, but not all laptops these days allow for this kind of upgradeability and the flexibility to make changes later as you get a feel for what your needs are. Hardware for adding a 2.5in drive is included in the box with the laptop, and there are step-by-step instructions for adding a new hard drive and RAM on the ACER support website that were very helpful. They did not, however, include the software stuff you’ll need to know if you’ve never added a hard drive before. After installing the new drive, search for how to get Windows to recognize the new hard drive. You’ll need to go into the system manager to initialize, format and assign a letter to your new drive before you can use it.

TL/DR: If you already live your entire life online and already pay to keep all of your information, documents, etc. in cloud storage or on an external harddrive and you're a big fan of google, this will be the perfect laptop for you and you'll love it. If you actually need/want anything on the computer itself - and to avoid the pile of monthly payments that come with totally online work/storage - this laptop will do nothing for you. review_title: Very good laptop for specialist needs, may have too many trade-offs for general workflows.
review_text:
My main job involves a lot of travel, and I do a lot of on-site computer work, which has meant that I bring redundant equipment with me to just about every site I work at. Importantly, this is not a computer that I would normally consider for this role, as while I require a decent amount of power, I've had bad luck in the past with gaming-focused laptops with the amount of wear-and-tear I place on a laptop, going through a Razer Blade and an XPS 15 in the last couple years. This laptop replaced an XPS 13 as my backup laptop, and so far has been holding up reasonably-well.

Importantly, I picked up this laptop during Cyber Monday sales, and at that time, the discount represented about a 35% discount compared to a competitively-priced alternative, if I was in the market to purchase a laptop at that moment. (and I deal-shop heavily when I look for laptops) So I may be comparing this product with a different value proposition than you may be.

Positives:
- Very strong specs for the price. It'd be nice if the internals were upgradeable to 32GB of RAM, but everything else here is _really_ good.
- The thermal design of the hardware pretty much means you can use the full power of the machine for long periods, and you don't need to worry about overheating. There are a couple on-site workflows where this laptop is the first laptop I'd be confident in it being able to handle for an entire day.

Negatives:
- For gaming, the screen is a good tradeoff. (a strong 1080p screen) For more general-purpose uses, though, this is the lowest-resolution screen I've purchased, either standalone or in a laptop, since 2011. Under normal circumstances, this is a disqualifying tradeoff for me.
- The device is built reasonably-well, but not as well as a MBP, an XPS, or a Razer Blade, and I've worn down 2/3 of those laptop classes over about 18 months of use. The bottom case dropping down especially concerns me, as it looks ripe for it to get caught on something at a bad angle, or for something to break via lateral forces from picking it up opened with in one hand.

Neutral:
- The cooling system at full-blast works really well, but is loud enough that you can't have a conversation while working in front of it.
- The built-in ASUS software is reasonably-good to the point that I wouldn't call it bloatware, but it sits somewhere between Dell (good) and Lenovo (better than it used to be but still meh) in annoyance level.
- You can charge and use it via USB-PD on the USB-C port, but if you're really going to be using it hard, you'll need the included 3lb power brick. Without it, at full blast, you're probably not getting an hour out of the laptop.
- The trackpad/numpad is clever, but it toggles based on the Numlock state on Windows. So, if you have a USB numpad (or keyboard with a numpad) attached, you can't use your external numpad + the laptop trackpad at the same time.

Overall, the main takeaway I want to give is that this is a very nice gaming laptop with some very specific quirks, but I bought it specifically because it's price point dropped so low that I could forgive some major personal spec problems because of the value it represented in other areas.

The bad:

I constantly end up at the bottom of the screen when I'm just trying to click on something. review_title: Does everything I want it to do, and well - which is keeping well over 20 tabs open simultaneously
review_text:
This is a great computer. I've had this a month; I just recently switched over to using a Chromebook for the first time after decades of using PCs.
My last PC laptop died after 18 months, and I've found that that is the typical lifespan for a laptop. I was sick of doling out $350-400 every other year, so I decided to try the Chromebook.

I suspect that this one will last longer than that. Let's go through the hits, then the single miss. The screen is bright; it is true HD; and the increase in detail from 1368 to 1920 pixels is amazing. The speakers are good and loud. As the title of this review says, I can easily keep well over 20 tabs open simultaneously without any problems whatsoever. I have 17 tabs open as I type this, and the computer is doing fine. I typically have far more open than that, though - approaching 30. The "hard drive" is an SSD = Solid State Drive, so there are no moving parts to this thing. It boots up in 10 seconds, flat. Amazing! The 32GB storage is enough, but you can open up a Gmail account and store your stuff in the cloud instead. (Gmail has

The keyboard has nice action to it. It comes with a wireless mouse, which works well, and is pretty cool - never had one before. The battery life is kind of insane! No, it's not the 12 hours advertised. But it's easily about 6 or so, and that's a huge leap over any of the PC laptops I've ever used. It's thin, it's light, it's metal. The thing just works, period. No crashes, no annoying "Windows must update your computer for the next hour." Chrome updates automatically in the background without my having to do a thing - as it should be.

The only miss, the only problem, of course, is that it doesn't run any software. Now, this really isn't a miss at all - this is how a Chromebook machine is designed from the get-go. But you have to really, really understand this going in before you make the switch to Chromebook. For me, there are only two programs that I ever run on my computer. One is Turbotax, and I know you can simply run that online, so that's not a problem. The other is a planetarium program called Stellarium - it shows you where all the stars and galaxies and such are. I've got a workaround for that, too, as it runs off-line. I've downloaded it to an old (2008) desktop computer, works fine. So, I'm all set.

My only actual complaint is the keyboard alignment. It seems shifted to the right about a half an inch, which messes me up. In other words, I'm a touch typist, and when I go to put my fingers on the keyboard, I find that I'm putting them in the wrong spot initially. As I've used the keyboard more and more, this is less and less of a problem, as I adjust to where the keys actually are.

It's a rather thin and light laptop obviously, so it seems they skimped on the cooling (Had an Aorus x7 briefly, same company, same case basically, more cooling pipes, worked a lot better). How do I know it has less cooling pipes? I fought with the extremely tight screws that almost wouldn't come out to take the back off and put a 2nd SSD in. review_title: Beautiful display. Good performance. No junk software.
review_text:
We got this for my husband, this is his review.

You won't find a better display on any laptop. Vizio's IPS 1080P LED back lit display is simply beautiful. The CPU and graphics performance are quite good, especially considering the price of the laptop. Its nicely styled and not bulky. It has only two USB 3.0 ports but that's good enough for most situations. The built in memory card reader is a must. It has no DVD ROM drive.

Windows 8 install is very clean. There is no "bonus" junk software installed like most of the major brands. This is my first use of Windows 8 and I'm not impressed, I see no point in giving an OS two graphical user interfaces. One is enough for anyone.

The hardware in the laptop is standard intel kit with HD4000 and Nvidia GT640M. The motherboard includes two DDR3 Dimm slots with two 4GB sticks installed which is up-gradable to two 8GB sticks which I'll probably do later. It has a tiny 32GB mSATA SSD which Windows 8 uses as a cache for the 1GB SATA spinning disk. It boots into Windows 8 in a matter of seconds. The mSATA SSD and hard drive are begging to be side graded to dual 256GB SSDs which would yield data throughput of a RAID 0 array of between 800 MB and 1 GB / sec for high end Samsung SSDs.

Linux installed easily with a Kubuntu boot USB drive (I run Gentoo). To boot linux the easiest solution is to install rEFIned, an open source EFI boot manager that recognized all OSes and an EFI boot-strap-able linux kernel which will load from rEFIned. I have not found a good way to get to the intel RAID BIOS setup. Setting Boot OS to "other" got me there once.

The laptop has a few drawbacks. The first laptop we received could not charge its battery. We returned it to Amazon without issue, the second laptop did not suffer from that malady. There is a review on another vendors site that talks about the same issue. Clearly this is a production problem for the device.

The keyboard is pretty bad. When I say bad, once in a great while it fails to type when a key is pressed and slightly more often will give two characters instead of one. I generally keep this laptop docked to an external USB keyboard so it doesn't matter to me, but it may become an issue when I take it on the road.

When pushing performance to the limits, the laptop gets uncomfortably hot, so perhaps the label "laptop" is a bit of a misnomer.

Even when idle the fan spins at low RPM. This might annoy some people, it doesn't really bother me.

I take its quirks because its display is unequaled. I'm looking forward to future designs from Vizio. If they deal with some of the problems I've listed here, I'll be a happy Vizio owner for years to come.

review_title: Decent little laptop. Shame HP choked the available graphics ram and put slowest drive possible in it.
review_text:
Pros –
Affordable, DDR4 Ram, Strong AMD APU, Nice touch screen operation, fairly light. Can handle older games ok.
Cons –
Poor modern title gaming thanks to company configuration, small battery, cheap material feels, glossy screen
Final Thoughts –
Recommended for price range, especially when on sale. Just don’t expect to do any heavy gaming because of hardware configuration. It’s a shame, too, since it has built-in potential to be a knockout buy.

Laptops have certainly advanced over the years. However, I am a power PC user. I like a tower packed full of the fastest components and a screen the size of a wall if I can get it. But ultimately, this is not the most practical solution when you are on the go or…writing a review in the backyard as I am now. Sure, I could have done this on my mobile phone; it is almost as powerful these days. Nevertheless, there is still a certain amount of convenience in a laptop that is not yet available in a mobile device.
Today I’m using HP’s Model 15-BA079DX laptop to write this. It was kindly provided by AMD and is powered by AMD’s newer A10-9600P processor. It comes packed with 4 cores of 2.4Ghz power accompanied by 6 more compute cores from the built-in Radeon R5 graphics. HP has included 6Gb of Samsung 2133 MHz DDR4 ram in this particular unit (Product W2M88UA#Aba) It’s equipped with standard ports including a USB 3.0 port, two USB 2.0 ports, a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack, an HDMI output port, and an RJ45 LAN port. There is a card reader on the right side, along with a Super-Multi DVD/CD burner. For connectivity, it features Bluetooth 4.0, Wi-Fi 802.11b/g/n, and 10/100Mbps Ethernet. It also has built-in HD webcam. Its thickness is around 0.9-inch and it weighs roughly 4.75 lbs. with a 3-cell Li-ion battery attached. I’m finding an average runtime of 1:45min to 2:15 hrs. depending on tasks performed. You’ll be cutting it close on a 2.5 hr. movie but it was doable off full charge.
DDR4 is a long-awaited upgrade for AMD fans: a processor that can run DDR4 ram. [Is this previous sentence redundant???] It is the latest, fastest, consumer version of computer ram on the market. This is kind of a big deal to those who know the inner workings of a computer. To those who don’t, it means faster computing and lower power requirements to do so. Essentially, it offers better efficiency all around, despite its small size.
The HP15, as I’ll call it, is a new budget-oriented device. It’s not a screaming fast-gaming laptop that you’ll have to plug in in 30 minutes, nor is it a stripped-down basic screen and keyboard. Boasting the aforementioned AMD APU and the newest format of ram, this laptop actually packs some punch. Web surfing is a breeze and quick; it has no extraneous page load times. Multi-tab browsing, even with Microsoft Edge, is effortless. Yes, that means this unit comes preloaded with Windows 10 64 Bit Home edition. It also is minimalist on bloat ware. Uninstalling these is easy enough and makes the laptop a little faster, since it has less to load up and run. I personally removed everything except the HP assistant (which I disabled) and the Cyberlink Video software for the occasional DVD playback.
Speaking of DVD’s, the screen on the HP15 is a multi-touch display sized at 15.6-inch with HD 1366 x 768 pixel resolution. The picture is clear and clean. But the biggest benefit is the tough screen capabilities. As I type along and make a mistake, I love the convenience of just pressing the highlighted word, and the correct spelling pops up. I then press on the correction and I’m done. There’s no messing with the track pad and it alleviates the need for a mouse when writing. The screen responds to a soft, rather than hard, touch. The caveat to this is the screen is glossy and makes working out in daylight difficult, as it just can’t seem to get bright enough to combat the daylight.
The track pad has a textured surface of injection plastic, as does the rest of the unit. It’s relatively responsive. In other words, it works, but I can’t comment much further, as I hate track pads in general and will always default to plugging a mouse into any type of device that allows it. The left/right click buttons carry a solid feel and satisfying click. The keyboard is the standard chicklet style. It offers not much key stroke travel. [Is this what you mean???] However, it’s laid out well enough for easy typing, even with my big hands. You also get a dedicated 10 Key setup allowing for easy number entry. The unit comes with the usual fn key features for controlling your audio, media playback, and even a dedicated “Airplane mode” key.
The shell of the laptop is injection molded plastic, but it is not very thick. For example, if you lift it one-handed from a corner of the unit, you can almost feel it flex under its own weight. I don’t think it is anything serious; however, although there is no separation of parts, it is definitely engineered to minimum tolerances. The top of the shell has a ribbed design texture to aid in grip when carrying. The rest is a smooth micro texture. While not necessarily a fingerprint magnet, it does seem to create a lot of darker colored area wherever your hands make contact, due to the transfer of your natural oils. It does clean up easily, though a quality soft cloth is advised for lint capture as opposed to paper products.
I mentioned productivity is a breeze. Facebook gaming, then, is no issue. On the flip side, AAA gaming is out. The HP-15 is not designed for it—period. So how about MOBA’s ? You might be able to turn all the options down and get some playability. I personally don’t play any MOBAs, so I have no results. I’m offering a calculated guess based on the specs here presented.
Quick DDR4: check. Strong AMD APU: check. Good AMD R5 Graphics: check. However, HP has decided, for whatever reason, to limit the available ram to the GPU to only 384mb. Most modern titles need at least 512mb to even fire up. Quick tinkering with the bios doesn’t allow this to be changed either. What a shame. If you could upgrade to 16GB of ram and if you could feed the gPU up to 1GB of shared ram, you could have a beastly, super economical portable.
Overall, if you’re looking for a sub-$350 all around laptop that is quiet with some neat features, this isn’t a bad a deal. It’s nothing stellar, but when the price occasionally drops below $299, it’s seriously worth considering. I’ve really been enjoying the touch screen for editing on the fly and can see me using this laptop a fair bit more than I thought I would.

Also, sometimes, there have been "glitches" with Chrome OS on it: freezes...hangs...crashes...

Mostly, I am impressed with what I received for the price I paid.

review_title: I hate to do this, but... (plus an update)
review_text:
I rarely leave negative reviews, but it's got to be said. I love the form factor, the removable keyboard, the handy flip/cover/stand BUT this thing just constantly freezes, restarts itself, etc. making it completely unreliable (I'm talking multiple times PER DAY). At this low price point, I certainly expected it to not be perfect and totally accepted the low pixel cameras, weak speakers and other low end features in exchange for being so affordable. I bought it for writing, surfing the net, watching youtube and sketching with a stylus - that's it (I don't even need it to have cameras or a touch screen). However, I I simply cannot accept that it just constantly fails. If this thing could stay up and running it would easily get 4 stars from me.

Lenovo should be embarrassed by this thing, it's definitely a dark stain on my perception of the company. Sadly, I have to say that if you think you're saving money by the low price, you're wrong - I will now need to buy another device, at higher cost, having basically wasted my money on this. Add the cost of this and the cost of a reliable replacement and I'd have been able to buy a high end tablet in the first place... but Lenovo got my money. I should have believed these reviews.

04/26/2022: For whatever reason, this thing has become much more reliable. It still freezes sometimes but it hasn't just died and rebooted itself in a few months. Possibly it's from updates, possibly because I limit it to 5 chrome tabs and no more than 3 apps (usually 2) running at a time. Either way, it has become a lot more useful since it stopped rebooting itself multiple times per day. Youtube still freezes up a lot but I am happier with it these days. Also, the speakers are pretty weak but I just run it through a bluetooth speaker if the washer is running or there's some background noise going on.

06/15/2022: This machine has continued to be more reliable. My main complaint now is the touch screen is a bit under sensitive to touch (I have very dry hands, so that may be it). It hasn't restarted in a long time (although it does freeze for a few seconds here and there). When using Sketch (drawing program for use with a stylus) it slows down and it seems to tax it but just regular youtube, web browsing, email, etc. it's pretty solid. Love the integrated stand/cover and detachable keyboard, too. It used to get very hot and doesn't seem to do that anymore so I have to believe an OS update along the way has fixed something. So, for the low price point it's ok.

So far so good. The laptop looks as good or better than anything Apple is putting out, at a much better price. The speakers are as good as you'll find in a laptop this size. This is touchscreen and the screen can swivel 360 degrees, something no Apple can do. The fit and finish feel fantastic and although it doesn't have a fingerprint sensor, it's not a big deal since you can sign in with Windows Hello--where it sees your face and infrared scans it. It usually works well and quickly. The touch-pad works almost as well as having a mouse.

The only things I would recommend would be to have more USB 3.1 inputs instead of 2 USB C's and maybe a quad core processor, instead of just a dual core. Also it would be nice if the laptop was a little slimmer, 4.4 lbs. isn't bad but it could be lower. Also take off more of the bezel on the screen, particularly at the bottom, kind of like the Dell XPS or Samsung 9.

If you get this laptop, you won't regret it. It's probably the best in it's class!
